title: Tortoise the Boaster
subtitle: Ogumefu's tortoise cycle and Ellis's name for it

learningObjectives.text: In Ogumefu's “Tortoise and Crab,” what ends the two friends' boasting?

tortoise-crab.author: Yoruba storytellers; collected and published in English by M. I. Ogumefu
tortoise-crab.translator: not applicable; authored in English by M. I. Ogumefu
tortoise-crab.locator: Legend XXXVII · TORTOISE AND CRAB; Legend XXXVII · TORTOISE AND CRAB, normalized characters 25-796
tortoise-crab.excerpt: EVERYONE knows that Tortoise and Crab are enemies. One morning on the seashore they decided to fight to see which was the stronger, but, as both of them are protected by a hard shell, neither could succeed in injuring the other. Finally they came to an agreement that they were equal in strength. “We are so well protected by our [p. 77] armour,” said Tortoise, “that no one can harm us.” “And thus,” said Crab, “we are the strongest creatures in the world.” But at this moment a boy passed by and picked them both up. Tortoise was boiled in a pot and his shell was made into ornaments, while Crab was cooked in a stew for the boy’s supper. Since that day the descendants of the two boasters have always been ashamed to meet, and that is why they always shun one another.
tortoise-crab.note: Verbatim English text from M. I. Ogumefu's 1929 collection, which his preface describes as belonging to the Yoruba country of Southern Nigeria. It is a Yoruba-authored retelling for readers, not an ethnographic record of practice.

tortoise-stories.work: The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa
tortoise-stories.author: A. B. Ellis
tortoise-stories.translator: not applicable; authored in English by A. B. Ellis
tortoise-stories.locator: Chapter XIV · FOLK-LORE TALES; Chapter XIV · FOLK-LORE TALES, normalized characters 19668-20149
tortoise-stories.excerpt: We now come to those tales which may be called "Tortoise Stories," since the tortoise (awon) always plays a leading part in them. The tortoise has, in these tales, various superhuman powers attributed to him, and, in most, is described as acting craftily or mischievously. He, in fact, fills in the folk-lore tales of the Slave Coast the place of the spider (anansi) in the tales of the Gold Coast, and which are in consequence known as Anansi 'sem (Anansi asem), "Spider Stories."
tortoise-stories.note: Verbatim English text from Ellis's 1894 survey of the Yoruba-speaking peoples. It is colonial-era ethnography: claims belong to Ellis's report, and his comparative and evolutionary framing is commentary, not community testimony.

narrativeBlocks.title: Two suits of armour
narrativeBlocks.body: In Ogumefu's tale, Tortoise and Crab fight to prove which is stronger, agree their shells make them unbeatable, and boast that nothing can harm them.

narrativeBlocks.title: The pot answers the boast
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Yoruba Legends; whitespace normalized): “EVERYONE knows that Tortoise and Crab are enemies. One morning on the seashore they decided to fight to see which was the stronger, but, as both of them are protected by a hard shell, neither could succeed in injuring the other. Finally they came to an agreement that they were equal in strength. “We are so well protected by our [p. 77] armour,” said Tortoise, “that no one can harm us.” “And thus,” said Crab, “we are the strongest creatures in the world.” But at this moment a boy passed by and picked them both up. Tortoise was boiled in a pot and his shell was made into ornaments, while Crab was cooked in a stew for the boy’s supper. Since that day the descendants of the two boasters have always been ashamed to meet, and that is why they always shun one another.”

narrativeBlocks.title: A shame that explains a habit
narrativeBlocks.body: A passing boy picks them both up: Tortoise is boiled and Crab is stewed. The tale ends etiologically: their ashamed descendants still shun one another.

narrativeBlocks.title: Ellis names the type
narrativeBlocks.body: Ellis's 1894 survey calls these “Tortoise Stories” because the tortoise (awon, also called ajapa) always plays the leading, crafty part, and says the tortoise fills the role the spider Anansi plays in Gold Coast tales.

narrativeBlocks.title: The collector's verdict
narrativeBlocks.body: Ogumefu, a Yoruba author, calls Tortoise “rascally” in his own preface and says readers feel he deserves his fate. The trickster is loved and judged at once, and Ellis's Anansi comparison shows the same trickster slot holding a different animal on a neighbouring coast.
